title: United States v. Florida East Coast Railway Co. (1973)
shortTitle: United States v. Florida East Coast Railway Co. (1973)
summary: A statutory direction to act after hearing did not require trial-type procedures for general prospective freight-car incentive charges.
notes: Rehnquist wrote for the Court; the district court was a three-judge court; the Supreme Court reversed.

sections.Parties: Two railroad companies, including Florida East Coast and Seaboard, challenged the Interstate Commerce Commission’s incentive per diem rates for use of freight cars owned by other railroads. The United States and the Commission defended the rule.
sections.Material Facts: Congress amended the Interstate Commerce Act to address chronic freight-car shortages and instructed the Commission to consider ownership levels and factors affecting supply. The Commission collected extensive railroad data, held an informal staff conference, issued proposed incentive charges, and allowed sixty days for verified facts, briefs, and objections. Railroads requested oral hearings and challenged the data and the charges’ distributional effects. The Commission considered their written submissions, modified aspects of the proposal, and adopted the rule without additional oral hearings.
sections.Procedural History: The district court set aside the rule because it considered APA § 556(d) applicable and believed the refusal to receive oral evidence prejudiced the railroads. The Supreme Court rejected that procedural ruling. Douglas, joined by Stewart, dissented and would have affirmed the district court.
sections.Issue: Did the organic statute’s requirement that the Commission act after hearing, together with specified substantive factors, trigger formal APA rulemaking under §§ 556–557? If it did not, did the organic statute nevertheless require oral testimony, cross-examination, or argument?
sections.Holding: The hearing language did not trigger the APA’s on-the-record requirements, and the written notice-and-comment opportunities satisfied the hearing requirement in this prospective general rulemaking. Equivalent statutory language could trigger formal procedures, but these words and substantive directions did not.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority relied on Allegheny-Ludlum’s interpretation of the same statutory hearing language. Directing consideration of certain factors constrains the decision’s substance without prescribing a trial as the means of collecting information. The APA itself recognizes hearings of different kinds and permits written submissions in some settings even when formal provisions apply. The railroads received the proposed rule, an opportunity to object, and consideration of their submissions.

The Court used Londoner and Bi-Metallic to distinguish an individualized factual determination from a broadly applicable prospective policy. The incentive rates applied to all covered carriers; unequal economic effects did not convert that policy choice into adjudication of each railroad’s circumstances. The railroads had asserted statutory rather than constitutional deprivation. Douglas emphasized disputed statistics, changed regulatory assumptions, serious financial consequences, and the need for an open hearing given the Commission’s broad discretion. The subsequent notes treat the majority’s rulemaking presumption as an interpretive approach rather than a constitutional prohibition on Congress demanding more procedure.

topics.lrs-o-hearing-trigger: A direction to act after hearing did not trigger formal rulemaking in this context; written participation fulfilled the hearing requirement.
topics.lrs-o-legislative-facts: The Court distinguished individualized determinations from general railroad-incentive policy and rejected the premise that a statutory hearing always required oral testimony.
topics.lrs-o-apa-classification: The Court's reasoning depends on classifying the incentive-charge proceeding as rulemaking rather than adjudication (the Londoner/Bi-Metallic line).
